title: Effects of gender and personality on experience of small living spaces: Ceiling height and floor plan shape in virtual environment
research_question: To examine whether place attachment to small living spaces is influenced by 1) ceiling height and floor plan shape, and 2) individual traits such as gender, age, and personality.

participants.description: 48 participants (26 men, 22 women) with ages ranging from 18 to 59.
participants.recruitment: Recruited through the Amazon Mechanical Turk website and an online participant recruitment tool on a university campus.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four 3D virtual mock-up walkthrough videos of small living spaces (236 sq ft each). Conditions varied by floor plan shape (short/square-like: 15'4"x15'4" vs. long/rectangular: 10'x23'6") and ceiling height (low: 7'6" vs. high: 9'6"). All spaces contained a bathroom, kitchen, and bedroom/living room area with identical interior elements (furniture, color, materials, equipment, lighting).
stimuli_or_exposures.source: 2.1 Virtual stimuli, 2.2 Four Small Space Conditions, Figure 2

measures.instrument: Adapted from Kaltenborn (1997), Kyle (2004), Gifford (2007), Raymond et al. (2010), Li & Han (2021); 11 items, 5-point Likert scale.
Subscale of Place Attachment (4 items, e.g., 'I identify strongly with this room.'), 5-point Likert scale.
Subscale of Place Attachment (3 items, e.g., 'This room is a good place for the activities I like to do.'), 5-point Likert scale.
Subscale of Place Attachment (2 items, e.g., 'I am willing to come back to this room.'), 5-point Likert scale.
Subscale of Place Attachment (2 items, e.g., 'I am very emotionally attached to this room.'), 5-point Likert scale.
Items from the Big Five personality survey (Ramstedt and John, 2007); 8 items, 5-point Likert scale.

findings.antecedent: Floor Plan Shape (short, square-like vs. long, rectangular)
findings.quote: floor plan shape showed a significant impact on the mean of place attachment (β = -0.165, t (45.1) = -3.38, p = 0.0009); that is, participants scored higher in place attachment for a space with a short, square-like floor plan than the space with a long, rectangular floor plan
Whereas ceiling height was not a significant predictor of mean place attachment

Ceiling height had a negative impact on place dependence (β = -0.09, t (40.6) = -0.88, p = 0.048). In other words, participants rated higher functional or goal-oriented connections to high ceiling spaces than to low ceiling spaces.

findings.antecedent: Floor Plan Shape (short, square-like vs. long, rectangular)
findings.quote: floor plan shape has a negative impact on place identity (β = −0.67, t (133.3) = -5.79, p = 0.01).

findings.antecedent: Floor Plan Shape (short, square-like vs. long, rectangular)
findings.quote: a significant negative floor plan shape effect on place dependence was found (β = −0.62, t (131.3) = 1.15, p < 0.05).

findings.antecedent: Floor Plan Shape (short, square-like vs. long, rectangular)
findings.mechanism: More affective bonding to a square space due to perceived openness.
findings.quote: Floor plan shape had a strong negative impact on personal sense of place (β = -0.91, t (131.3) = -0.74, p = 0.0003); participants had more affective bonding to a square space than a long rectangular space.

findings.antecedent: Floor Plan Shape (short, square-like vs. long, rectangular)
findings.quote: Participants reported a lower partial sense of place after viewing the long floor plans than they did after viewing short floor plans; floor plan shape showed a negative impact on the partial sense of place (β = -0.62, t (131.3) = -1.42, p = 0.032).

findings.mechanism: Extroverted individuals may prefer larger personal spaces or have different needs for spatial connection.
findings.quote: Extroversion was found to have a significant negative impact on place attachment (β = -0.59, t (6) = −2.66, p = 0.0086).

findings.mechanism: Extroverted individuals may have different self-place relationships.
findings.quote: extroversion had a negative impact on place identity (β = -0.86, t (6) = −3.7, p = 0.0003)

findings.mechanism: Extroverted individuals may have different functional needs or preferences for space.

findings.antecedent: Higher Extroversion AND High Ceiling Height
findings.mechanism: More extrovert participants felt significantly more functional connections to high ceiling spaces than low ceiling spaces.
findings.quote: Extroversion had a positive impact on place dependence for high ceiling spaces (β =0.16, t (41.0) = -0.76, p = 0.039); that is, more extrovert participants felt significantly more functional connections to high ceiling spaces than to low ceiling spaces

findings.antecedent: Men AND Longer Floor Plan Shape
findings.mechanism: Gender differences in spatial preferences for longer floor plans.
findings.quote: Gender and floor plan shape showed a significant interaction effect on place identity (β = 0.18, t (41.0) = 0.76, p = 0.001). Men reported significantly more positive impact on place identity with longer floor plans than women.

findings.antecedent: Older Age Group AND Longer Floor Plan Shape
findings.mechanism: Older age group perceived longer floor plans to be more functional than shorter ones.
findings.quote: The older age group thought that the spaces with long floor plan shape, which is rectangular in shape, were more functional than the spaces with short floor plan shape (Table 9).

findings.antecedent: Higher Extroversion AND Short Floor Plan Shape
findings.mechanism: More extroverted participants had a more positive impact on personal sense of place with the short floor plan than the long floor plan.
findings.quote: More extroverted participants had a more positive impact on personal sense of place with the short floor plan than the long floor plan (Figure 4C).

findings.antecedent: Men AND Longer Floor Plan Shape
findings.mechanism: Men reported significantly more affective ties with longer floor plans than shorter ones.
findings.quote: Men reported significantly more affective ties with longer floor plans than shorter ones (β = 0.18, t (41.0) = 0.76, p = 0.001).

findings.antecedent: Older Age Group AND Longer Floor Plan Shape
findings.mechanism: Older age group reported a lower partial sense of place after viewing the long floor plans than they did with the short floor plans.
findings.quote: older age group reported a lower partial sense of place after viewing the long floor plans than they did with the short floor plans (Table 10).

mechanisms: People feel more connected to a small living space when the plan is more open than a long linear one.
The psychological benefit from the slightly increased openness with a square-like plan could override the advantage of a long floor plan with separated kitchen and bedroom areas and enhanced privacy.
implementation_implications: Provides useful information to decision-makers, developers, and policymakers for improving the quality of tiny homes.
Offers end users of small affordable housing or refuge shelters more comfortable experiences.
Suggests considering user trait differences (gender, personality) to provide more satisfying resident experiences in small living spaces.

limitations: The study's scope was limited to ceiling height and floor plan shape; other design elements like furniture and windows were not included.

The virtual reality technology used may not offer fully 'lifelike experiences', potentially impacting the generalizability or reliability of findings, though the authors frame this as an opportunity for future research with more sophisticated VR/AR.

paper_metadata.title: Effects of gender and personality on experience of small living spaces: Ceiling height and floor plan shape in virtual environment
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Effects of gender and personality on experience of small living spaces: Ceiling height and floor plan shape in virtual environment
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Virtual reality (VR) technology has been used as a design research tool to enable a virtual experience of space as a real-life-scale mock-up. In terms of user experience design research, VR is highly scalable and adjustable, meaning that designed virtual prototypes and environments can be tested on a diverse population without restrictions. In spatial design, VR has been applied in various contexts, often focusing on behavioral intentions and psychological perceptions. Small living spaces are gaining more popularity as an affordable housing solution and an environmentally sustainable lifestyle. Despite their growing demand, user experiences of small living spaces have not been empirically tested. Specifically, the impact of users’ different characteristics on the psychological responses to small living spaces has rarely been studied. In this study, we used three-dimensional (3D) virtual mock-ups to test how subjects of different genders and personality types perceived different shapes of a small space. A 2 × 2 factorial design was used to test two different wall length-width combinations (short vs. long floor plan shape) with two different ceiling heights (low vs. high). Forty-eight participants were randomly assigned to watch one of the four small living spaces. After watching the virtual walkthrough video, participants filled out the questionnaires on their perceptions. The results show that floor plan shape had a significant impact on place attachment. Participants reported greater place attachment to the space with a shorter floor plan than the longer one. In addition, higher ceiling height is closely related to functional and goal-oriented connections. The impact of the floor plan shape of the space on place attachment differed according to gender, age, and personality. Participants with higher extrovert scores reported greater functional connections to higher ceiling height. Men reported significantly more affective ties with longer floor plans than shorter ones. The older age group perceived longer floor plans to be more functional than the shorter ones.
